title: The hindrances arrive
hookLine: desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt: five visitors every sitter meets

lines: A CRAVING. A FLASH OF IRRITATION.
cards: A sudden craving for something sweet. A flash of irritation at the neighbor's music. A heavy, sleepy fog.
A restless itch to get up and check something. And a quiet voice asking: is this even working? Sit with the breath for a while and some of these may show up.
Meeting them doesn't mean you're doing it wrong. The Pali texts list all five, side by side, and give them one name.

teach.b: That name is nivarana, a hindrance: something that blocks the view. One: sensual desire, wanting pleasant things. Two: ill will, irritation, aversion.
Three: sloth and torpor, the heavy, dull, sleepy mind. Four: restlessness and worry, the buzzing mind that can't settle, and the nagging regret.

teach.h: FIVE VISITORS, FROM DESIRE TO DOUBT.
teach.b: Five: doubt, the wobbling mind that can't commit. In a discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha gives a picture for each, using a bowl of water you're trying to see your face in.
Desire is water mixed with dye: everything gets tinted.
Ill will is water boiling. Dullness is water covered in moss. Restlessness is water whipped up by the wind.
Doubt is muddy water set in the dark. Each time, you can't see your reflection clearly. But the water itself is fine.
It's what's in it, for now.

The first thing the tradition teaches about the hindrances is simply to recognize them. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, when sensual desire is present, the meditator knows: sensual desire is present.
When it's absent, they know it's absent.
Before any remedy, you name it. Why does that help? Because a visitor you've named is no longer running the house.
Restlessness you've noticed is just restlessness. Restlessness you haven't noticed becomes you, getting up to check your phone. So think of the hindrances as visitors, not enemies.
They knock, they come in, they eventually leave. Your job is to see who's here.

how: Buddhist meditators learn to recognize the five hindrances when they arise, noting their presence or absence, as the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness describes, before applying any remedy.

o: something that blocks the mind's clear view
a sin that must be confessed and undone
a special power you unlock by sitting

games.q: the hindrance and its water — tap the pairs.
p: water whipped up by the wind

s: meeting the hindrances means you're meditating wrong
the texts list them as things a meditator learns to recognize, not as signs of failure.
the first step with a hindrance is to fight it off
the discourse begins with simply knowing: this hindrance is present.
doubt is pictured as muddy water in the dark
you can't see your reflection clearly.

games.q: you're sitting, and a strong itch to get up and check your phone arrives. what does the discourse say to do first?
games.why: the first step is to recognize it: when restlessness is present, the meditator knows it's present.

practice: Each time the mind wanders, before coming back to the breath, ask which visitor this is, wanting, irritation, dullness, restlessness or doubt, and name it softly: ah, restlessness.
If none is here, notice that too: no restlessness now. Don't fight them and don't feed them; just see who's here, and come back.

wordCard.voice: Nivarana. A hindrance, something that blocks the view: the five visitors a sitter meets.

orig.note: Pali: a hindrance, something that blocks the view.

carryVoice: Your line: name the visitor. Under the dye and the mud, the water itself is fine. Day one hundred and fifteen, complete.
